The early life stages of Perna canaliculus are characterised by a brief embryonic period during which fertilised ova develop into free-swimming veliger larvae. Egg energy content averages approximately 0.0004 joules , although median values are slightly lower at 0.0003 J and the full range extends from 0.00007 to 0.003 J. At 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the age at birth for late D-larvae is roughly 5 days [ab = roughly 5 days], a stage coinciding with the development of the PII layer and the onset of exogenous feeding. The corresponding shell length at birth in these late D-larvae is 0.00979 cm [Lb = 0.00979 cm], while the dry weight at birth reaches approximately 1 × 10⁻⁶ grams , a value derived from length ratios between 2-day and 4-day old D-larvae. This dry mass increases markedly as the larva transitions through subsequent developmental milestones, setting the stage for the morphological transformations that accompany settlement and metamorphosis.

The transition from a planktonic to a benthic existence is marked by larval metamorphosis, a critical juncture in the life cycle of the New Zealand green-lipped mussel. At 19.1 °C [T = 19.1 °C], the time since birth at metamorphosis is approximately 15 days , following an embryonic period of roughly 5 days as noted above. The shell length at metamorphosis, representative of competent pediveligers ready for substratum attachment, is 0.028 cm , a figure slightly exceeding the 0.0242 cm reported in some earlier studies. Attendant to this shell dimension, the ash free dry weight at metamorphosis is only 1.8 × 10⁻⁶ grams , underscoring the minimal somatic investment present at the point of larval-juvenile transition. These minute dimensions belie the rapid growth trajectory that characterises the subsequent juvenile phase, during which the mussel must accumulate sufficient tissue to support eventual reproductive function.

Juvenile Perna canaliculus grow rapidly following settlement, and the attainment of sexual maturity is governed by both size and thermal conditions. The shell length at puberty, an estimate based on spawning records from Alfa2001, is 2.7 cm [Lp = 2.7 cm], a size that falls within the lower portion of the 3 to 60 mm range observed during peak spawning months. At 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the time since birth at puberty is approximately 150 days [tp = approximately 150 days], a duration that reflects the species' capacity for relatively early maturation under optimal growing conditions. The corresponding dry weight at puberty, calculated from unpublished NIWA length-weight data, reaches 0.5 grams . Under thermal regimes of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) typically exhibits a value of 14% [GSI = 14%], although this index is known to vary substantially both across seasons and among different geographic localities.

Reproductive output in reproductively active adults is prodigious, reflecting the species' status as a broadcast spawner with high fecundity. At a water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the maximum reproductive rate corresponds to an estimated approximately 27,400 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 27,400 eggs per day], a value underscoring the enormous gametic investment required for successful fertilisation in a turbulent marine environment. The ultimate total length that these mussels can attain is 24 cm [Li = 24 cm], representing the upper limit of shell growth observed in natural populations — a dimension that places Perna canaliculus among the larger mytilid species. Correspondingly, the ultimate dry weight of large adults can reach 35 grams , a substantial mass that supports a high gonadal output over successive spawning seasons. These dimensions confer a competitive advantage in terms of fecundity relative to smaller-bodied congeners.

Longevity in Perna canaliculus reflects a life-history strategy that balances high early reproductive output against a modest maximum lifespan. Under typical thermal conditions of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], maximum life span is approximately 7300 days [am = approximately 7300 days], which equates to roughly 20 years in the absence of significant predation or disease pressure. This extended potential lifespan, combined with the high daily egg production described earlier, results in a lifetime fecundity that can exceed several hundred million eggs per individual. Individuals from populations inhabiting warmer northern waters may experience reduced longevity relative to their southern counterparts, although comprehensive age-validation studies remain scarce. The species' capacity for both rapid juvenile growth and sustained adult reproduction exemplifies a flexible life-history repertoire that has facilitated its success across a broad latitudinal gradient along the New Zealand coastline, from the subtropical waters of the north to the cooler temperate regions of the South Island.
